title: Communicating final results to parents clearly and compassionately
description: A practical guide for Kenyan school principals on communicating end-of-term and end-of-year results to parents — especially when results are disappointing — in a way that maintains trust.
body:
How a school communicates results shapes the parent relationship as much as the results themselves. A strong result communicated poorly can feel like an afterthought. A disappointing result communicated with care and a constructive path forward can actually strengthen a parent's trust in the school, because it demonstrates genuine partnership rather than a purely transactional relationship.

Timing and framing matter

Results released with no context — a report card alone, with no accompanying communication — leave parents to interpret the numbers without guidance. A brief accompanying message, explaining what the results show and what support is available if needed, gives parents a constructive frame rather than leaving them to draw their own, sometimes alarmed, conclusions.

Communicating strong results

Even positive results benefit from genuine, specific acknowledgement rather than a generic congratulatory message. A note that highlights a specific area of improvement or achievement, rather than only the overall score, reinforces to parents that the school is paying genuine attention to their child as an individual, not just processing numbers.

Communicating disappointing results constructively

The instinct when results are disappointing is sometimes to soften the message so much that the actual concern is lost, or conversely to be so direct that parents feel blamed or alarmed. The more effective approach names the concern honestly, places it in context (a specific subject, a specific pattern, not a vague overall judgment), and immediately follows with what the school is doing or recommends to address it.

A useful structure for difficult results conversations: State the specific concern factually. Explain what the school has observed about possible contributing factors. Propose a specific next step — a meeting, a support plan, a referral. This structure avoids both minimising the issue and leaving parents without a constructive path forward.

Inviting a conversation, not just delivering a verdict

A results communication that explicitly invites parents to discuss concerns — rather than simply stating the outcome — signals genuine openness to dialogue. Parents who feel they can raise questions or concerns about results without feeling dismissed are more likely to engage constructively with whatever support the school proposes.

Using the Parent Portal to give context, not just numbers

A results notification that directs parents to a portal showing not just the current score but the trend over recent terms gives far more useful context than an isolated number. A student who improved from BE to AE this term, even if not yet at the desired level, is a different conversation from one whose score has been static or declining — and parents should have visibility into which pattern applies to their child.

Following through visibly

When a results conversation leads to an agreed support plan, following up with the parent after a reasonable period — did the plan help, does it need adjustment — demonstrates that the school's concern was genuine, not just a formality attached to a difficult conversation.

Give parents real context, not just a score.
